Vignette:
# Arjun

Arjun was twenty-three when he was stopped by police outside a convenience store in Queens. He had ducked in for milk on a Friday evening, and when he came out, an officer called him over. There was a report of a robbery two blocks away, the officer said—a man matching his description. Arjun, whose family had lived in America for fifteen years and who had never been in trouble, explained this calmly. He was cooperative. He stood still as the officer patted him down, his hands moving across Arjun's chest and ribs and legs with a methodical pressure. It was cold that night, unseasonably so for October, and Arjun remembers the officer's hands as cold too—the shock of them through his thin shirt, the grip firm and impersonal. A second officer arrived. They told him to turn around. They told him to put his hands behind his back. He did. The cuffs were metal and tight, and they took him to the precinct, where he sat in a holding cell for eight hours before his mother came, before someone checked the store camera and saw that he had been inside the store when the robbery happened three blocks away.

The case was dropped. But something in Arjun had fractured.

In the months that followed, he returned to his job as an editor at a small publishing house in Manhattan, and he tried to move forward. He married Priya, a woman his parents had introduced him to, and they found an apartment in Forest Hills. But the world had become a place of hidden threats. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he was incapable of handling what life demanded of him. When he thought about that evening—about the pressure of the officer's hands, the cold seeping through his clothes, the smell of the precinct's fluorescent-lit holding cell, a chemical tang he could not quite name—grief would flood through him so completely that he could barely breathe. His body would remember the position he had held in those cuffs, his hands locked behind him, and he would feel his shoulders draw back and his spine curve inward, as if the memory were not something he was recalling but something happening to him again.

The triggers came without warning. A cold hand on his shoulder—Priya touching him on a winter morning—sent him spiraling. Being alone with Priya in their bedroom became impossible. He would find reasons to leave the room, to stay late at the office, to sleep on the couch. He could not explain to her why her presence, her closeness, felt dangerous, felt like it was pulling him toward something he could not survive. When she tried to talk to him about it, when she sat beside him on the bed and asked what was wrong, he felt the edges of reality beginning to dissolve. He would feel unreal, as if he were watching himself from outside his body, and the panic that followed was worse than any physical sensation.

At work, his ability to focus had deteriorated. He would be reviewing a manuscript and suddenly smell the precinct again—that chemical, metallic odor—and lose twenty minutes to the memory. His supervisor had begun to notice. Last month, he had missed a deadline for the first time in four years. His supervisor, a woman, had called him into her office to discuss it. Sitting across from her, he had felt the dissociation creeping in at the edges of his vision, and he had made an excuse and left. He had not been back to the office since.

It was Priya who finally insisted he see someone. She was crying when she said it, frustrated and frightened in equal measure. She told him that nothing he did seemed to help, that he was pulling away from her, that he seemed to believe nothing good could ever happen to him again. She was right. Arjun knew she was right, and knowing it only deepened his conviction that he was broken, that he had failed at the most basic task of being a functional human being. He was terrified of what a therapist might tell him, but he was more terrified of losing Priya, of confirming that he truly was incapable of holding onto anything that mattered.
